subtopic: TRIBUTE TO FORMER GOVERNOR GENERAL OF CANADA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO FORMER GOVERNOR GENERAL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of this house and all Canadians of our generation who have vivid personal recollections of Canada's all-out war effort during the first half of the forties were grieved to hear this morning of the death of the right hon. the Earl of Athlone.
As governor general of Canada through the most hazardous years of the war, the Earl of Athlone won the confidence and the affection of the Canadian people from coast to coast. The Earl of Athlone entered on his high office in the dark days of 1940 when the future of civilization might seem to have been at stake. Throughout the following anxious years until his departure in the spring of 1946 His Excellency performed the complex and difficult duties of governor general with tact, with zeal and with distinction. From the first the Earl and the Princess Alice threw themselves wholeheartedly into the life and problems of our country. By their wide travels over Canada, by the warm-hearted way in which they greeted thousands upon thousands of Canadians and by the active interest which they took in every phase of Canadian life in wartime, in our armed forces, in munitions plants, in hospitals and in countless other directions, they did all that was in their power to help promote the feeling of national unity so essential to a total war effort.
The Earl of Athlone had had a long and admirable career of public service before he came to Canada. As a young officer, he had served with distinction in the campaigns both in Matabeleland and in South Africa. It was indeed his devotion to his duty as a soldier which prevented him from coming to Canada as governor general in 1914, when he was appointed to that office by His Majesty King George the Fifth. Instead, he went to France, again to serve with distinction in Britain's armed forces.
Throughout his long career, and particularly as governor general of Canada, he showed an exceptional appreciation of the
82715-19J
manner in which the commonwealth of nations was developing as a free association of independent nations, bound together by a common loyalty. In his speeches he frequently interpreted that development with sympathy and skill.
No one could have shown greater pride in the part which Canada played in the war, and in the place which Canada had earned by her efforts among the united nations, than did the Earl of Athlone in his many public addresses as governor general of this country.
Each time I have had the pleasure of meeting the Earl of Athlone and Princess Alice since 1946, and I have had the privilege of doing so on several occasions, they never failed to show continued interest in Canadian events and developments. I know too that many other Canadians who have had the privilege of meeting them have had the same experience.
The passing of the Earl of Athlone will be widely mourned throughout Canada, as throughout all the commonwealth. He will long be remembered for the ability and devotion with which he performed the duties of his high office at a most critical time in the history of our country and of the civilized world.
I would like, supported by the Leader of the Opposition, to suggest that as a tribute to the memory of this great public servant of his sovereign, of Canada, and of the commonwealth, and as a mark of our deep sympathy with Her Royal Highness the Princess Alice, with our beloved Queen and with all the members of the royal family we stand together for a moment of silence and mournful reflection on their bereavement.
(Whereupon the members rose and observed a period of silence.)
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) with regard to the much discussed and all-important, though I must admit somewhat technical, question of interest rates. I wish to ask him

Inquiries of the Ministry a question based on what he said on November 27 last, and I read briefly from what he then said, as reported at page 47 of Hansard:
It is not the action of the Bank of Canada which is causing the rise in interest rates, it is the demand on the money supply both in business and in government circles; and the Bank of Canada interest rate is only a reflection of the increased interest rates in the money market.
And again:
Question.

I will ask the question in due course. Then he said:
When it is said that the Bank of Canada rate was increased and thereby other rates were increased, it is just merely putting the cart before the horse because it is the reverse.
Order.
There seem to be many speakers in this house, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And this is a time when it is not proper for speeches to be made.
Mr. Speaker, having laid the foundation for my question, does the Minister of Finance not think-
You have laid a foundation for a 10-storey building.
If hon. members across the way kept quiet they would understand the question.

Does the minister not agree that the interest rates in the money market, of which he says the Bank of Canada rate is only a reflection, are themselves affected by the Bank of Canada's own action in buying and selling bonds in the open market, and that therefore the Bank of Canada does influence interest rates?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the hon. member for repeating what I said; it is very seldom that I find myself an authority on anything. But it is only just what he said, Mr. Speaker; it seems to me that most members of the Tory party start with the foundation of the Liberal party and then see whether they cannot get somewhere after that.
If we used the foundations of your party we would never get anywhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think I can answer the question very simply by saying that I have no change to make in the statement I made then, though it was in answer to a question during the question period. I would be glad to discuss it in greater detail later at the appropriate time. However, since it is a matter of interest and since my hon. friend has


gone to some trouble to look for my remarks on the subject, may I say there is no question at all that the interest rate, the rediscount rate, of the Bank of Canada, which was increased, my recollection is, in August 1955, followed after a steady increase in interest rates which had extended over six months prior to that. To that extent and for that reason I gave the answer in November that the increased discount rate is merely a reflection of the increased demand for money in the money market which led to an increased interest rate.
Now then, it may be that when the Bank of Canada increases its interest rate certain persons may ascribe to it-that is, the increase in rate-reasons why they in turn should increase their interest rates. That does not at the same time admit that there is any validity for certain interest increases for that reason alone and I think that probably is what my hon. friend had in mind.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I like to use moderate language but I think the minister, as he did last autumn, is simply not answering. I would like to refer the minister to what the governor of the Bank of Canada said at page 383 of the proceedings of last year-
Question.
-and I think the minister will find that it is entirely in disagreement with what he said. I would also like to remind the minister-
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. gentleman has had time enough to lay a long foundation and frame a long question and unless he wants to ask a supplementary question at this time I do not think he should do so by laying down another long foundation.

Mr. Speaker, to return to my previous question, may I ask the Minister of Finance this question. Is the minister persisting in his previous statement that the Bank of Canada has no influence on interest rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have never said that the Bank of Canada had no influence on interest rates. My recollection is that that question was asked of me in a different form by the hon. member for Greenwood a month or so ago and that I did not make any answer which would indicate that the Bank of Canada could not influence interest rates. As a matter of fact, it could do so. He knows that and I think everyone else knows it.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of ihe Opposilion):
speechtext: In that connection, would the minister outline what powers the Bank of Canada has to do other than control the quantity of credit? What power has it to allocate credit? What power has it to give advice and to apply pressure to private business, if that course is being followed? I ask the minister whether the government has abdicated to the Bank of Canada its rights, its authority, and its responsibility to do things that are not justified by the Bank of Canada Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have said already this afternoon that I intended to make some rather extended remarks about this matter. But in anticipation of doing that, I think I should answer my hon. friend by reminding him that I told his acting leader, in answer to a similar question some months ago, that if he would only read the Bank of Canada Act he would get the answer to his question.

In
view of the advice I received from the Minister of Finance on that occasion, Mr. Speaker, I might ask a supplementary question. Does the government approve of the Bank of Canada's decision to restrict credit independent of collateral and, as my leader has suggested, thereby more or less controlling business generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am afraid I do not quite understand that question, Mr. Speaker.
Have you read the Bank of Canada Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have read the Bank of Canada Act several times.
May I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he might read the Bank of Canada Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have done so.
[Later: ]

I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance supplementary to the question asked by the hon. member for Greenwood. If the minister wishes the house to understand that the Bank of Canada is a follower rather than a leader, what steps is the government taking to meet the inflationary trend at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I must say I am gratified that hon. members of the opposition are now agreeing that we have an inflationary problem. There was a time not so long ago when they questioned the things that were being done. I can only assure my hon. friend that to the best of my ability in the course of this session I shall deliver quite
Inquiries of the Ministry a long speech on this particular subject in order to try to tell them the answer to that question.
[Later: ]

I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Are the chartered banks of Canada authorized or advised by the Bank of Canada to charge different rates of interest to different borrowers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.

It is true, however, that they had to pay the high interest rate for raising the money already discussed this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. What is the attitude of the government in regard to the Gordon commission's recommendations that the government pay the cost of relocation for people who wish to move away from the neglected maritime provinces?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My impression of some of the reports made by several newspapers with respect to that aspect of the Gordon commission report is that they are quite inaccurate. The suggestion, as I read it in the report, is that everything possible should be done to bring the economic activity of the Atlantic region up to a point where the standards of living there will be very much nearer those of the most favoured regions in Canada. If after doing so it should appear that the resources of the area are not sufficient to accomplish that for all those who are in the area, and some of them wish to remove for that reason to other areas, I take it that the suggestion is that there should be consideration given to assisting them in making that move. But that is only in the event that all possible ways of making the best possible use of the resources of the area and to the fullest possible extent have proved insufficient to raise the standards of living of the people in the area

close enough to those of the people of the most favoured regions in the country.
Mr. Speaker-
A supplementary question-
Oh, oh.
Two leaders.

speechtext: Will the Prime Minister tell the house how effective the representations have been, and whether there is any intention to go ahead this year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The premier of New Brunswick and the people of New Brunswick will require no backing of their bonds for the Beechwood development. With respect to other developments, there have been no reports submitted that would establish that there is prepared a project that would have economic possibilities and economic result's. That is being carefully considered and when it is demonstrated that' there can be use made of water power if sufficient can be obtained to make it an economic proposition or that there can be thermoelectric power produced with the use of coal in the Atlantic region, then if the province of New Brunswick requires assistance to bring that about their request for assistance will be given very sympathetic consideration because I think it is in the interests of the economy of the whole of Canada to have no depressed areas in Canada.

I should like to ask a supplementary question. What excuse has the government for refusing over the past two years to accede to Premier Hugh John Flemming's request for assistance to back his power development?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think I am better informed of the attitude of the government of Canada and of the government of New Brunswick than is my hon. friend. I have been having conferences with the prime minister of New Brunswick ever since he became prime minister.
And you turned him down flat.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not turned him down flat. As soon as they bring forward a scheme which can be studied to determine whether it has economic possibilities and which is apt really to stimulate the economy of the region it will receive careful consideration, and that matter is still being studied by the advisers of the government of New Brunswick.
May I ask a supplementary question? May we expect a decision on this before the next election?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
You can
expect a decision on it just as soon as there is put before us by the government and people of New Brunswick a scheme that can be studied as to its economic merits.
Does the Prime Minister deny the fact that on at least three occasions we have put forward such schemes?

speechtext: I do most positively deny that there has ever been put forward the kind of scheme that could be implemented along the lines I have mentioned. Are
the Prime Minister and his government going back to the days of the thirties when Mackenzie King made the statement that there would not be a single nickel given to the provinces?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was going to ask the Minister of Justice for the statement which, since he is on his feet, he is probably now going to make.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO INCREASED PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, namely the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, asked me the following question:
In view of the recent increases in the price of newsprint will the minister ask the restrictive trade practices commission to investigate the circumstances of these increases and determine whether there are any elements of price fixing or restraint of trade?
By way of reply to that question may I say that since it is the practice of the director under the Combines Investigation Act to consider notable price changes with a view to making sure that they are not the product of collusion, it is not necessary for me as minister to ask the director to investigate the price changes in newsprint to which my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has referred in his question. If there is any reason to suspect collusion, the director conducts an inquiry, but as the hon. members know, it is contrary to the usual practice to disclose whether such an inquiry is being conducted until the report is presented.
At this point I think I should emphasize the fact that the combines branch, of course, has no authority to regulate prices. Its function is to investigate those situations in which there is reason to believe that the firms in an industry are co-operating to keep prices above the level which current market forces 82715-20
Inquiries of the Ministry would support. In a time of stationary or falling costs and demand, a general and uniform price increase would be regarded with suspicion. In the present time of rising costs and strong demand, such increases may be explained on the basis of ordinary market behaviour and are not in themselves evidence of collusion. On the basis of these price changes, therefore, the director does not feel he would be warranted in conducting an investigation.
When the director does not see fit to begin an inquiry on his own initiative, I can, of course, direct him to do so; but for the same reasons that he has given, I see no justification for taking such a course.
I think I should also say that no requests for an inquiry have been received by my department from any United States authorities.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Seeing that the wholesale price of sugar has risen sharply again in the last week, would the minister please inform the house whether this rise is the result of unfair practices or whether it should be due only to the world shortage?

speakeroldname: Hon. Sluarl S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED INCREASE IN WHOLESALE PRICE
speechtext: In accordance with the practice to which I referred just a moment ago of noting price changes in various markets, the combines branch has been observing recent increases in the price of refined sugar. These price increases appear to be directly related to increases in the cost of raw sugar. It would appear that some variation exists in the degree to which the refiners in eastern Canada have increased their refined sugar prices. It would also appear that world raw sugar prices which started to advance in early November have advanced more rapidly and to a significantly greater degree than have the selling prices charged by the refiners. The combines branch does not, therefore, regard these present increases in refined sugar prices as significant in relation to the anti-combines legislation.

maintopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED INCREASE IN WHOLESALE PRICE

that in peacetime only a provincial legislature can authorize such a course. All the branch has power to do is to prevent collusion, and where there are market conditions which more than explain the increase in price it is quite difficult to suspect collusion.

speechtext:
On Monday the hon. member for Oxford asked a question concerning motor propelled craft on inland waters and I should like to give a reply to it now.
In order to obtain the opinions and suggestions of interested persons, a questionnaire was sent out to a large number of yacht clubs, power squadrons, canoe associations, fish and game clubs, provincial governments, manufacturers of boats, outboard motors, etc. and to editors of boating magazines, and to individuals who had expressed interest.
The replies to these questionnaires are now being analysed in the department, following which it is intended to call a meeting of representatives of organizations and other individuals who have expressed a wish to attend. It is hoped that as a result of this meeting it will be possible for the department to formulate the policy to be followed in the making of any new regulations.
In the meantime the minor waters navigation regulations, which provided a penalty for dangerous operation of motor vessels in the minor waters of Canada, have been amended to be effective in all Canadian waters and to increase the possible penalty from $200 to $500. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested last Thursday to hear certain remarks made by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Enfield). On that occasion he made the following statement, as reported at page 100 of Hansard:
I know I can report very accurately that public opinion in my constituency, and I think everywhere in Canada, is enthusiastic in its acclaim of the stand taken by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this crisis.
The word "crisis" of course, Mr. Speaker, refers to the crisis and the situation in the Middle East. Now, while the hon. member for York-Scarborough may be very well satisfied as to the attitude of the people of Canada generally on this matter, I for one would like to tell him-and I am sure many hon. members will also tell him-that the people are by no means satisfied or content with the stand taken by the government on this matter. More than that, there are a great many questions in the public mind which remain unanswered. It is for this reason that during my time in this debate I wish to deal with three matters concerning the foreign policy of this country.


The first of these matters is, what is the keystone of our foreign policy? Second, we should have a clarification of certain attitudes of the Canadian government toward the United Kingdom and the commonwealth generally. The third matter has to do with certain matters relating to the United Nations emergency force.
As I say, the first matter is, what is the keystone of our foreign policy? The day before yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) pointed out that there are four factors that influence our foreign policy, and I think no hon. member in this house would disagree that these are certainly the four most important factors. They were, as I recall them, our relationship with the United Nations; our relationship with the commonwealth; our relationship with NATO; and our relationship with the United States of America.
The question that naturally arises is this: Which of these four cornerstones is the keystone of our foreign policy? In other words, on which stone does the security of Canada chiefly stand, since security is the aim of foreign policy? If the government has decided which of these factors is the strongest in effecting our national security, is it not foolish to pursue activities in other fields of foreign affairs that undermine the keystone of our security? For example, just recently we have had a conflict, an obvious conflict, of interests in our foreign policy. We have had the government taking a certain stand in the United Nations which had a very adverse effect on two of our chief NATO partners, namely, the United Kingdom and France. In any event, the government has not made it clear, I am quite sure, on which stone of these four cornerstones our security chiefly stands, and that is something which should be made very clear because it is bound to happen-it happened last October and November and is bound to happen again- that we are going to be faced with the dilemma of which horse to ride, on which base of our foreign policy we are going to rely. We are going to have to make a choice sooner or later. The making of the choice caused a great deal of trouble and embarrassment to the government last fall and may do so again.
While it is quite true that all four of these factors are important, there must be one of these factors, or a combination of one and another, on which our foreign policy must chiefly rely for our own security. I think the government should make this very clear; I think the people of Canada want to know just what it is.

It is undoubtedly the view of many people in Canada that our foreign policy must have two aspects: the long run and the short run. With respect to the long run, we recognize the United Nations is a body designed to expand among all the nations of the world the rule of law, mutual understanding and trust, and we certainly agree that we should accept our responsibility in furthering the achievement of those ideals. But I think we all realize, Mr. Speaker, that at the moment the United Nations still leaves much to be desired with respect to effecting Canada's national security.
We have all seen what happened in the Hungarian situation. The Russian government has absolutely refused to obey the wishes of the United Nations, and certainly at the moment the United Nations has no permanent force with which to enforce its decisions, whether they be decisions of the security council or of the general assembly. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, in so far as the short run is concerned, we cannot rely at the moment for our immediate security on the United Nations. This is an ideal which we must work for in the long run. We must try to achieve the ideals of the United Nations but, for the short run, we must rely on other places for our national security, namely, NATO and the commonwealth. I for one, Mr. Speaker, do not feel that we should do anything in the United Nations or elsewhere which would undermine and destroy our partners in NATO and I think there is very little doubt about that because it is on these two organizations that our national security chiefly relies at the present time.
I have no doubt that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) who, unfortunately, is not in his seat at the moment, will reply to these remarks and say: We cannot have any broad principles; we have to deal with each situation as it arises. No doubt he will say that. That may well be the truth, Mr. Speaker, but we still must have guiding general principles and objectives on which to base our foreign policy.
The second matter that I should like to deal with is that of clarification of certain attitudes of this government toward the United Kingdom and the commonwealth generally. For some time the emphasis of Canadian foreign policy seems to have been on the United Nations, and I would almost say that the United Nations would seem to be the cornerstone of our foreign policy. Maybe it is. We will anxiously await an answer from the government. Then, we have heard, of course, a lot about NATO and our relationships with the United
The Address-Mr. Nesbitt States. We have heard very little for a long time about our relationship with the commonwealth except, Mr. Speaker, for the last few days, because I think the government has now realized that certain decisions that were made last fall, despite what the hon. member for York-Scarborough said about the activities of the government, are not popular in Canada generally with respect to the problem in the Near East and Middle East.
I bring this matter up because certain questions have arisen in the public mind as to what the attitude of this government really is to the commonwealth and the United Kingdom. In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the January 14, 1957 issue of Life magazine. I might say that I do not always by any means agree with editorials that appear in Life magazine or Time magazine, but nevertheless these are very large publications, with great sources of information at their disposal, and they are considered by many to be very reputable and authoritative magazines.	.
The editorial in Life magazine is headed:
Who Stopped the Suez Invasion?
In other words, why did France and Britain withdraw? I quote from the editorial:
As for Eden's motives, one among many was conclusive: he received a concrete threat that the British Commonwealth would be dissolved within a matter of hours-and dissolved permanently- unless the fighting was stopped. India and Ceylon were particularly insistent; Canada only a little less explicitly threatening.
That is the kind of thing, Mr. Speaker, that cannot help but raise doubts in the minds of the people of Canada. When a publication such as Life magazine, with great sources of information, comes out flatly with a statement like that, I think it most certainly should be replied to by this government; otherwise the people of Canada cannot help but entertain the gravest doubts concerning just what are the government's policies. I am sorry to say it, Mr. Speaker, but this article in Life magazine cannot help but be given certain support by the attitude the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) took in the house last November 26. The remarks made by the Prime Minister on that date have been referred to by many hon. members in this house. At that time he categorized the activities of the British and French in the same way in which Russian activities can be categorized and his now famous remarks about the supermen of Europe revealed the Prime Minister's ill-concealed delight concerning the trouble in which Britain and France found themselves. Such attitudes cannot help but give rise to editorials such as the one carried by Life magazine.
302	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nesbitt
On November 26 last, the same date, in reply to a question which had been proposed by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) with respect to an exchange of correspondence between the Prime Minister and the then prime minister of Great Britain, the Right Hon. Sir Anthony Eden, the Prime Minister refused to disclose the content of his message. Finally as a result of questioning in the house the Prime Minister read the correspondence he had with the Right Hon. Sir Anthony Eden. The letter which was read into the record appears at page 23 of Hansard for November 26 last and I do not propose to take the time of the house by reading it now because hon. members can refer to it. It is quite clear from that letter, however, that the Prime Minister virtually requested Sir Anthony Eden not to give him permission to disclose the content of their exchange of correspondence. The reasons for this can best be judged by the people themselves when they read the record.
The reluctance of the Prime Minister concerning making public this exchange of correspondence is a very strange thing because President Eisenhower had no hesitation in making public the message he sent to the Right Hon. Sir Anthony Eden, but apparently the Canadian Prime Minister was not anxious to do so despite the fact that he denied there was a shred of truth in the alleged fact that he sent a stinging rebuke to Sir Anthony Eden over the activities of the British in the Suez area. For this reason one question must be uppermost in the minds of most people and it is this. Just what is Canada's position in relation to the commonwealth. Canada's support of the Asian bloc of the common-* wealth as against the United Kingdom, which is one of our principal allies in NATO and one of the principal cornerstones of our immediate security in the world, suggests a conflict of interests on the part of Canada which cannot help but arouse suspicion, doubt and wonder in the public mind.
I would also like to deal with the matter of the United Nations emergency force. This is going to consume a number of minutes and I hope I will be able to complete my remarks in the remaining time allotted to me. Since the government of Canada has accepted credit for establishing this United Nations emergency force, the government must also accept the responsibility in very large measure for the results that have been achieved by this force.
The first question I would like to ask is this. What are the objectives of this force?
I will briefly refer to the Canadian resolution of November 4 last which reads as follows:
Requests, as a matter of priority, the secretary general to submit to it within 48 hours, a plan


for the setting up, with the consent of the nations concerned, of an emergency international United Nations force to secure and supervise the cessation of hostilities in accordance with all the terms of the aforementioned resolution.
The words "aforementioned resolution", of course, refer to the cease-fire resolution and to its proposal at the United Nations. Has this resolution achieved its purpose? I would say yes; in one sense of the word and to the extent that the hostilities have ceased in Egypt, the United Kingdom and French forces have been withdrawn and fighting, at least for the moment, has stopped. But, and there is a very large "but", has not the plan which was submitted by the secretary general tended to do three things in addition to that? These are as follows: (1) To humiliate, cause loss of prestige and injury to the United Kingdom and France, two of our most important NATO allies. (2) To place Egypt in a position to dictate to the United Nations and thus greatly enhanced the prestige and power of Nasser in the near East-Nasser being the avowed enemy of the West. (3) As a result of the first two items I have mentioned it has made the ultimate solution of the mid East and near East problems just as difficult as they were before and in fact has probably rendered them more difficult, thus increasing the danger to world peace.
In this regard I would like to refer very briefly to the remarks made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) yesterday in this house. I do not intend to repeat them because they can be found in Hansard of Tuesday, January 15 at page 236. It was very well pointed out by the hon. member that the United Nations force had unquestionably been subject to dictation from Egypt. I do not intend to repeat the hon. member's remarks because they have already been placed on the record, but I would point out they have not as yet been denied. However, there is another matter which I think is just as important a reference as that made by the hon. member for Kamloops. In his remarks the hon. member for Kamloops referred to a recent editorial in the New York Times and I would like to refer to a publication which a great many hon. members of this house receive. I refer to the Commentary on Foreign Affairs which is issued by the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. I have in my hand the issue covering the period from September 15 to November 30, 1956. It refers to the situation in the Near East and at page 8 the following appears:
There followed Mr. Hammarskjold's visit to Cairo to make practical arrangements about the stationing of the police force (now styled U.N.E.F.) about communications and supplies-and to discuss with President Nasser its functions and the measures to be taken for clearing the blocked canal. The original resolution of 2nd November had specifically

stated that "upon the cease-fire being effective, steps be taken to reopen the Suez canal and restore secure freedom of navigation". In the proceedings on 7th November, however, when a further resolution was passed, the secretary-general committed himself to the idea that the general assembly "could not request the force to be stationed or operate on the territory of a given country without the consent of the government of that country", an idea for which there is no warrant in the U.N. charter. It meant, as indeed the secretary-general's report to the ordinary general assembly showed, that Colonel Nasser was virtually allowed to make his own conditions. Thus, first, Egypt laid down certain rules as to the composition of the force: no Canadian army regiments because their uniform and military appearance would look too much like British troops, no contingent from Pakistan as a signatory of the Baghdad Pact, and so on.
I cannot help but feel that this house and the people of Canada have been at least partially misled by the government with respect to the purpose of this force. I would like to refer to a speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on November 27, 1956 as reported at page 61 of Hansard. At that point the Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
The function of this force which is now in being is to secure and supervise the cessation of hostilities, as I pointed out this morning, and carry out its task in accordance with directions received from the United Nations, not from any one member of the United Nations.
Further on he said:
The most important function is, of course, the policing of the zone between opposing forces in Egypt in order to prevent the recurrence, if possible, of the fighting.
He continued:
This force will stay in Egypt until the United Nations decides that its functions are discharged,-
And so on. Then the Secretary of State for External Affairs continues a little later, as found on page 61:
But that does not mean, as I understand it- and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, this has been made very clear in meetings of the advisory committee- that Egypt or any other government can determine by its own decision where the force is to operate, how it is to operate or when it must leave. Furthermore, the right of Egypt to consent to the admission of a United Nations force to its territory does not imply the necessity of consent to the admission of, or the right to reject, separate units or elements of that force. That is a stand, Mr. Speaker, which the Canadian representative on the advisory committee has taken.
Then the Secretary of State for External Affairs elaborates on that at some length. There is one thing that I think must be very clear to almost anyone and that is that the secretary general of the United Nations and apparently our Secretary of State for External Affairs have taken the attitude, and I think wrongly so as I will show in a moment, that the consent of Egypt had to be obtained to station troops there, that this consent was a mere something that just had to take place at one
The Address-Mr. Nesbitt moment of time and that if they once got consent they could put a force into the country, put it wherever they liked and do what they liked. That, Mr. Speaker, is plainly ridiculous.
Consent obviously implies a continuing state of affairs, not just one isolated consent obtained from Egypt. It is a continuing consent that is required. In other words, if, after certain troops had arrived, Egypt had said that she did not approve of them, would not have the United Nations force there any more and withdrew her consent, in view of what has been said by Mr. Hammarskjold and our Secretary of State for External Affairs the United Nations could not do anything else except withdraw the force if it did not continue to suit Egypt.
I repeat that consent is a continuing state of affairs, not just one isolated incident where you say to somebody that they can go ahead and do something. Clearly that is not what happened at all. It would be ridiculous to suggest that consent meant anything else. The secretary general of the United Nations, so far as can be seen, did misinterpret the purpose of the United Nations resolution of November 2 when setting up his plan, thus placing Egypt in a very favoured position. The plan devised by the secretary general and indeed the whole attitude of the United Nations seemed to sympathize with Egypt and thus placed the United Nations in a position of adjudicating upon the rights and wrongs of the situation, which it most certainly should not have done under the terms of the resolution.
The United Kingdom, France and Israel removed their troops and obeyed the United Nations, and these countries now have little or no voice with regard to the disposition, make-up or anything else concerning this special emergency force whereas in fact Egypt most certainly does. I should like you to inform me, Mr. Speaker, how much time I have left.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I
should like to show the members of the house in some detail how the secretary general of the United Nations has erred in his interpretation of the way in which this force was to be established and also how, as I have already mentioned, this house was more than slightly misled by the government as to the function and purpose of the force. First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the original resolution passed by United Nations on the 2nd of November, 1956. I will not read the whole resolution. If any hon. members wish to get it, they
304	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nesbitt can obtain it in the same way I did. I will read the cogent parts of it. The general assembly, after expressing its grave concern over developments in the Near East, went on to say:
1.	Urges as a matter of priority that all parties now involved in hostilities in the area agree to an immediate cease-fire and, as part thereof, halt the movement of military forces and arms into the area;
2.	Urges the parties to the armistice agreements promptly to withdraw all forces behind the armistice lines, to desist from raids across the armistice lines into neighbouring territory, and to observe scrupulously the provisions of the armistice agreements.
The armistice agreements referred to are the armistice agreements between Egypt and Israel made in the past. Then it goes on:
Urges that upon the cease fire being effective steps be taken to re-open the Suez canal and restore and secure freedom of navigation.
As I have already mentioned, Mr. Speaker, a couple of days later Canada introduced a resolution which I have already read but I will read it again as it is very short:
Requests, as a matter of priority, the secretary general to submit to it within 48 hours a plan for the setting up, with the consent of the nations concerned, of an emergency international United Nations force to secure and supervise the cessation of hostilities in accordance with all the terms of the aforementioned resolution.
Later on the secretary general of the United Nations submitted a report as to how the force would be made up, and I will refer to that in a moment. The final resolution which Canada supported is a rather lengthy one and it deals, of course, with the establishment of this force. There are two parts of it which I think are very cogent and should be referred to. They are found on page 2 of the resolution and this of course refers to the general assembly of the United Nations.
1.	Express its approval of the guiding principles for the organization and functioning of the emergency international United Nations force as expounded in paragraphs 6 to 9 of the secretary general's report;
2.	Concurs in the definition of the functions of the force as stated in paragraph 12 of the secretary general's report.
Then it goes on in more detail setting up the force, but the important parts are the two to which I have just referred. Let us see for a moment what paragraphs 6 to 9 and paragraph 12 of the secretary general's report contain. What they contain is very interesting indeed and certainly not what the people of Canada or hon. members of this house expected the function of the force would be. Paragraph 9 of the secretary general's report reads as follows:
Functioning, as it would, on the basis of a decision reached under the terms of the resolution "Uniting for Peace", the force, if established, would be limited in its operations to the extent that consent of the parties concerned is required under

The Address-Mr. Fairey United States and others to the detriment of the United Kingdom and France.
All these matters that I have raised have caused much concern and worry to the people of this country and I think they require an answer. I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when he returns from the United Nations, or alternatively the Prime Minister himself will deal at an early date with the points I have raised because these are questions of great public concern.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first and pleasant task is to offer words of congratulation to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) on the competent job they did in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. May I at the same time extend congratulations to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Die-fenbaker) on his elevation to the important office of leader of Her Majesty's official opposition. I know what a tremendous task he has undertaken, and I wish him well.
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to devote the greater part of my time to a report on the activities of the Canadian delegation to the UNESCO conference which was held in New Delhi, but before doing so there are one or two matters which have been mentioned in the speech from the throne and on which I would like to offer some comments. After all, we are supposed to be debating the speech and the amendments to the motion and perhaps it is necessary to justify one's time here by doing just that. I am grateful for what the speech contains and hopeful for what it does not contain.
First of all, the fact that we are to amend the Municipal Grants Act will bring some relief and help to at least two of the three municipalities in my riding. The city of Victoria itself and the municipality of Esquimalt will get considerable relief in their municipal expenditures.
Then the longed-for establishment of the Canada Council is something which pleased me greatly because one of its duties or that of one of its committees is to undertake the task of acting as a national commission for UNESCO. It might interest hon. members to know that of the 80 member states of the UNESCO organization, until a few months ago only three were without a national commission.
Another point mentioned in the speech from the throne is the proposal to grant federal aid to technical education. For me that is the most significant item in the address. On every possible occasion, I think

every time I have spoken in this house, I have urged that something be done for that class of workers who should comprise the skilled artisans. As I have pointed out on other occasions, in our training program there is a great gap between, on the one hand, general secondary education and, on the other hand, university education for those who are entering professional ranks. In between those two groups we have large numbers, in fact the vast bulk of our population, who ultimately are to provide the trained workers, the skilled workers, the artisans. The training facilities for them, up to now, have been extremely inadequate. I am therefore greatly pleased to note that the federal government is to increase the grants which formerly were given for this purpose.
While I rejoice that the universities are to be treated so generously, it is my hope that when the sum of money which is to be assigned to technical education is announced it will be equally generous, or at any rate generous enough to indicate that this problem is to receive significant attention. This perhaps might be a bombshell but it has always been my hope, and it still is, that some day the federal government will take over the complete responsibility for technical education, and that some day the federal government will build several technical colleges throughout this country so we may be given the opportunity to train the unskilled workers and make them into real artisans, and not be obliged to continue to rely on immigration for our trained supervisory personnel. Up to now that has been the rule in Canada. We need to give to our own Canadian people the opportunity to be trained to occupy those positions.
I know that in the preliminary report of the Gordon commission-and I know it is only a preliminary report-this subject is touched upon at pages 108 and 109, but there is not much there; it is treated rather casually. As a matter of fact, what is in it might just as well have been copied from any of the annual reports of the Department of Labour. In fact there is a fuller report in the latest issue which hon. members will have received, namely the annual report of the Department of Labour of March 31, 1956. It devotes several pages to this highly important matter. When the full report of the Gordon commission comes out I hope it will be found that they have given more adequate treatment to this subject and have made certain definite recommendations in that regard.
Since I mentioned immigration and the matter of immigrants, I think it is only fair that I should say a word about the activities

of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and commend him for his prompt action in going to Austria and making arrangements for the early entry into Canada of such a vast number of Hungarian refugees. It was something that I think the whole country applauded when our minister acted so promptly, and I hope he will receive the necessary recognition.
We assembled for this session, some of us with difficulty, at the time of the C.P.R. strike. Our transportation system throughout the country being disrupted as it was, the economy of the whole nation was affected. It is encouraging to know that this strike is over. I think that has come about owing to the wisdom and foresight of our Prime Minister who no doubt used his charm as well as his tact in bringing together the parties to the dispute, and who was not hurried into precipitate action. We are all highly gratified that the matter has been settled in a way which we hope will become permanent.
Having said all that, Mr. Speaker, I wish to spend the rest of my time talking about the ninth general conference of UNESCO which was held, as I said before, in New Delhi, India. It was my good fortune to be a delegate from Canada to this conference. The conference was held in November and part of December. I wish to thank the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs for giving me the opportunity to go there and increase my knowledge of other people, to widen my horizons and to join with my colleagues in making what I think was a significant contribution to the work of the association.
This association is one of the instruments of peace. UNESCO-the United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organization-is ten years old. It now includes 80 member states. At the conference, which opened with 77, three new ones joined, namely Finland, Morocco and Tunisia, so now there are 80 member states. That fact is rather significant, when delegates from practically every nation in the world meet together and join in friendly discussion. It exists because its members believe that the way to peace is by fostering a more complete understanding of one another, and that this objective can be achieved through education, science and culture. When one attempts to assess the value of this vast and sprawling organization-and that is what it is-and is inclined to be critical of its apparent slow progress, one should remember that the road to peace is rough and thorny, and that the nations of the world have different traditions, different religions, different backgrounds and
The Address-Mr. Fairey different customs; in fact, they are different. That fact is something to remember.
Here I want to say also that one of the important duties of the members of a delegation is to get to know the delegations from other countries. That is why so much importance is attributed to informal meetings, and we had many of them including group meetings at lunch time, in hotel rooms, at receptions, and informal consultations. That is where you get to know people. It is there that one gets to know that people have different approaches to the same problem, and learns to be tolerant. That is why I so greatly appreciated what the Prime Minister said in his speech on Wednesday last. You will find it Mr. Speaker, in Hansard of January 9 at page 33, at the top of the page in the left hand column:
I think this is something that we all have had to learn. Human nature and the essential aspirations of human nature are very much the same all over the world, but the background against which you have to place the attitudes of different people must be the background of their own civilization. . . .
That statement touched a responsive chord, because it took me back to New Delhi and reminded me of the different races and the different people we met there and the strange -to us-attitudes that some of them took on some of the problems we were discussing. The delegates-and I should name them, of course-were as follows. We had Leonard W. Brockington as chairman, and I wish to say something more about that fascinating gentleman in a moment or two. As deputy chairman we had His Excellency Mr. Morley Scott, the Canadian high commissioner to Pakistan; Senator Donald Cameron, former director of extension of the University of Alberta and still the director of the Banff school of fine arts; Mr. Lionel Bertrand, the hon. member for Terrebonne, Quebec, and my colleague in this house, and myself. Let me say that there was absolutely no difference between the delegates and the alternates with respect to the duties which were involved. We shared the duties quite fairly among us.
The alternate delegates, then, were Mrs. Florence Bird, whom everyone knows under the name of Anne Francis, the distinguished radio and press commentator; Dr. Leon Lortie, one of the distinguished chemists from the University of Montreal; Professor Jean C. Falardeau, head of the social science department, University of Laval; Mr. Freeman Stewart, executive secretary of the Canadian education association and Mr. John Parkin, a distinguished Toronto architect and president of the Canada arts council. So you see, Mr. Speaker, the delegates were chosen, with the exception of myself, of course, rather

The Address-Mr. Fairey wisely because they represented the various aspects of the work of UNESCO, the various sciences, arts and cultures.

speechtext: So does the hon. gentleman.
