speechtext:
We also had with us Miss Mary Dench of the Department of External Affairs and Mr. Mel Clark, whom we called the financial watchdog from the Department of Trade and Commerce and who is now stationed in Geneva. Miss Dench has been responsible for some time for all UNESCO matters in the Department of External Affairs. She is a most competent person and an indefatigable worker. Sometimes I thought she should ease up and play a little bit but she would not do it. I would say this, that she contributed to a remarkable degree to whatever reputation for competence the Canadian delegation had. The same is true of Mel Clark. He knows his way about international conferences, and he had no hesitation in looking for new paths to information which would be of value to us. He is a very competent person.
Anyone who knows Morley Scott, who I am glad to say is a graduate of the University of British Columbia, will not expect me to say much more than that he was an admirable second in command. He was cool, shrewd and wise, and his advice was invaluable. Finally, we had that most charming person, the high commissioner to India, Mr. Escott Reid. He did everything imaginable for us to make our stay in India enjoyable. He saw to it by arranging luncheons, dinners and so on, that we met particular people, people from all over the world and particularly people from India; people we ought to get to know if we were going to do a good job. He finally gave a most illuminating briefing based upon his intimate knowledge of India and the Indian people. He is a great Canadian.
The government of India made splendid arrangements for the conference. They built, if you please, a special hall, a vast place called-I have to consult my notes to pronounce it-Vigyan Bhavan, which is in the form of a theatre with a large stage, a big proscenium arch and a vast sloping floor. Provision was made for simultaneous translation into the four official languages. In addition there were two large conference halls also equipped for simultaneous translation. There were also the committee rooms.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it was a fascinating experience, and one is tempted to continue with a description of the people, of the many things we saw and places we visited, the sights and sounds of New Delhi and the surrounding district; all the things they have, but mostly the things they have not. However, I must report on the conference itself. We


met as a delegation every morning and sometimes during the lunch hour to go over the agenda for the day, decide on the policy we would adopt, what was to be said and who would say it. We met frequently to report. We were all given special tasks; that is, the tasks of attending various meetings were divided amongst those whom we thought were most competent to attend particular discussions. For my sins I was allotted the exchange of persons, technical assistance and administration. Mr. Freeman Stewart, who is a distinguished educationist, was on elementary education; Mrs. Bird was on mass communication, and so on. We were dodging about from meeting to meeting as the various subjects came up for discussion.
First of all, at this conference there were a number of plenary sessions which all attended. Then after that the conference broke up into two main commissions, the administration commission of which I was a member along with several others, including Mr. Scott, Mr. Clark and others who came in as their subjects were called, and the program commission. You see, therefore, how simple the organization is; and it works simply, in that one group of people are discussing items which are proposed as projects for the ensuing two years and the other group are discussing how they are going to meet the expenditures. It is in these two commissions that the detailed work is done. I shall describe it, perhaps not fully but in a little more detail later.
I want to return now to the first plenary session and the first day or two. Here, Mr. Speaker, I am trying to give hon. members an idea of the atmosphere and the change of attitude one gets as one discusses various matters. The conference opened at the time of the Suez trouble, which has been discussed by the hon. gentleman who preceded me. It was not a happy time for us. We had practically no information. Every morning the Indian papers were full of scathing editorials condemning the British and the French. Everybody was rather tense, particularly when the conference opened with a speech by the Indian minister of education, who was not too kind in his remarks about what he called the aggressors. As hon. members know, at conferences of this kind the speeches of welcome are sometimes described as blah, blah, but these were not. They were rather nasty from our point of view, and particularly when member after member from the Latin American countries, Egypt, Brazil, the south Asian countries and Russia went one after the other to the podium and repeated the same stuff. We sat there and took it. It was not a very happy time for the United Kingdom delegation, for any of us for that matter. The point I am trying to make is that I am not

blaming them one little bit. It was a time of tension, and people were speaking without too much thought.
However, the atmosphere was charged with something that should not have been present at a conference on education. It was recognized by some that this was no place for discussing the Suez matter. The place for that was in the United Nations itself, not in a conference supposed to be devoted to greater understanding through science, education and culture. Therefore it was in that atmosphere that the delegate for Canada was called upon. Of course Canada enjoys a great reputation. I am sure every hon. member in this house will agree that we enjoy that reputation because of the magnificent work of our Secretary of State for External Affairs. Although I do not like to say it in his presence, the Minister of National Health and Welfare also has contributed to it to a degree. There is no doubt about it, wherever you go in this world the name of Mike Pearson is known. It was because of that fact, and because of the unique position of our country, that when the delegate for Canada was called upon he had added importance.
So Mr. Leonard W. Brockington rose. Most of you know him and know what a fine speaker he is, with a wonderful command of English and a knowledge of how to put it together. Of course he looks a little imposing, because everybody knows he is crippled. He was helped to the podium, and the place was hushed. He made a magnificent speech. Well, perhaps I was prejudiced, because I arrived at a close friendship with him. I am positive that all who were there will agree that he raised the tone of the conference and brought it back to where it should be. If I might I should like to read just a couple of extracts from what he said. He commenced by paying the usual compliments and reciting the purpose for which UNESCO existed. Then he said, speaking about the tensions that then existed:
Above all liberties, said one of the world's greatest voices, is the liberty to know, to utter and to argue freely according to conscience. Perhaps we can all take some comfort from the knowledge that even today no stronger criticism of the disputed policy of the British government, no freer or more vigorous denunciation of its dangers has anywhere been spoken or written than in famous British newspapers freely published in Britain itself, in public meetings freely assembled in Britain, in earnest debates freely held in a free British parliament and wherever men gather in Britain to hammer out the truth on the anvil of free discussion.
And I may say, and perhaps not without malice, that he emphasized the word "free" every time he used it. I have another extract and this will be the last although I had intended to read more. He said:
The Address-Mr. Fairey
We in Canada who are the beneflciaries of the gifts of so many other peoples believe that there is only one race in the world which is really important and that is the human race. We are determined to pay with reverence our debt to humanity.
While I pay this tribute to our leader, I do so because I am convinced that he prevented the conference from getting off to a bad start.
Because of our reputation much was expected of us, so much so that later, when the session was all over and it was decided to have a final plenary meeting, with one speaker to speak for each of the four groups of nations, all those who spoke English combined to request that Mr. Brockington be the speaker for the English-speaking peoples, and he then made another magnificent speech which was the envy of all and which has been demanded by the press of the world.
Another thing that perhaps stemmed from Canada's reputation, and perhaps from our own good work, was the fact that when they needed a rapporteur for the great and important program provision they asked Canada to supply one, and it was most competently dealt with by Senator Donald Cameron.
To give the house some idea of the importance of this and what our attitude to it should be, I should like to say something about the resolutions at one of the plenary sessions. The director general of the secretariat prepared a program which they proposed to put into effect in the succeeding two years, and alongside it they had the budget, which was an estimate of its cost. That was placed before the conference. It had already been circulated to member states, and we had the right either to amend it or to pass it. But then, out of the blue, came a resolution from the floor that the budget be increased by $1 million. It was already up to nearly $1 million, but the resolution from the floor was to the effect, just let us have another $1 million.
Now, we were astounded because we are not used to doing things that way. We usually want to know what it is for. By the way, France seconded it. The question was, why do this now? The secretary general has not asked for it. My attitude, as an old civil servant would be, no; let us decide whether we have something that is worth doing and then get the money for it, and not get the money first and try to find some way of spending it.
There was a long discussion, but it was passed. It was passed because of the principle of one nation, one vote. The vote of Monaco is just as strong as that of the United States, which pays 30 per cent of the total cost of the
310	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fairey budget. I think Mr. Clarke, who is our financial adviser, told me before I left that the votes of those who supported the resolution were by people who paid only 15 per cent of the cost of the UNESCO program. However, it was passed immediately. I think there were 130-odd resolutions from the floor, all pressing various projects which were not in the program, and most of which were passed.
I said I was going to say a word or two about the two commissions. First of all there was the administrative commission which deals with all questions relating to the budget, the staff of the secretariat, the salaries and the financial and business administration of UNESCO organization. Then there was the program commission, which deals with all the projects, technical assistance, fundamental education, mass communication, all these things, and the individual projects all over the world. They decide which are valuable and which are not, and they pass them. At the end of the conference these two commissions meet together to try to get some kind of agreement between the two, and I may say that we did not get much agreement because so many projects were passed that the budget just would not meet them. It was then left to the executive to decide. I shall come to that again in a moment.
There is a belief in Canada and elsewhere that UNESCO needs overhaul. The attitude of Canada was that the administration was slack, and we emphasized need for greater efficiency. We stated that in all our work here we are used to expecting a reasonable degree of efficiency and integrity in everything we do with public funds, and we would like to see that in the UNESCO organization, but we were not quibbling particularly about the cost. We were prepared to be reasonably generous but we insisted that what funds were voted be wisely spent. We suggested, as did others, that UNESCO should concentrate on a few large projects. That does not necessarily mean two or three but a few well thought out projects which were designed to further the aim of UNESCO, which is mutual understanding, and not to dissipate its energies on a variety of projects all over the world. And so we either presented appropriate resolutions in the appropriate commission, or we supported those that were made by others.
The main resolutions for which we were responsible were first of all-and here I was going to use a slang expression but I will not use it in Hansard-
It is a good one.

We did not get it through but we got a modification of it. We proposed that we call in a firm of business consultants


to examine the procedures in the secretariat itself. This was not in any way criticism, because we know the difficulties; when you try to harmonize the views of representatives of 80 member countries, you have a job on your hands. And so we said, "You have existed for 10 years and it might be that somebody from outside might be able to point out more efficient ways of doing things"; but the secretary general did not buy that. He would not accept a firm of business consultants at all.
What we finally passed was a watered-down resolution. I must say that Mr. Clarke was mainly responsible for this one, although I had to do some of the talking on it. We finally got it through in this form. A number of business experts would be borrowed from a number of member states, not too many, who were not connected with the organization of UNESCO, and they would do this survey job on the secretariat.
I neglected to mention that the next conference two years hence will be held in Paris, and in all likelihood all future conferences will be held there because they now have a permanent home. There was much criticism throughout the conference concerning the cost of the new building which is nearing completion in Paris. The building apparently cost more than was estimated. Mr. Parkin, who was the delegate responsible for this subject, offered a good deal of criticism of the methods used in granting contracts and paying commissions and in authorizing extras. We did not get very far, but at any rate we let them know there were people watching it.
I have already told you there were over 100 resolutions from the floor, many of which referred to projects which could not possibly have been discussed in detail in a large conference although the sponsors insisted that these be discussed. Senator Cameron I think was responsible for a change, as program rapporteur. The procedure in future will be that when any country wishes to suggest a project as being worth while in the interests of the objectives of UNESCO it will send notice to the secretary at least six months prior to the next conference. Then, in order to satisfy those who want to speak from the floor, it was decided that any projects proposed in the conference itself should be discussed but passed on to the next conference two years hence. Although there were many other points, these of course are just the main ones. We were deluged with paper. I think each of us must have had a stack several inches high. This cost a lot of money, because each paper was published in four languages. Some suggestions were made in the

program commission, if I may put it this way, to stop the avalanche of paper and simplify the procedure.
I have tried to build in your minds a certain attitude toward UNESCO in order to show that while we certainly believe its administration could be improved, we must also recognize the difficulties involved. These nations are scattered all over the world, and I might say we have a great deal to learn from those nations with which we are not too familiar. We can learn more from them than they can learn from us.
The question arises as to whether we wish to be considered as a country that is always critical, and as to whether we are too much concerned with efficiency. One gentleman with whom I spoke and whose name I shall not reveal said to me, "You Canadians are always talkings about efficiency and integrity. I am more concerned with good will and good relations". It occurs to me that perhaps he is right, and certainly you get that impression while attending one of these conferences. Is it not worth while that we and the other western nations tolerate some things we do not like very much for the sake of good will and improved relations?
Canada, I think, must decide between giving guarded support-I was going to say reluctant support but I do not mean quite that- and admitting that there are practices we cannot accept, agree to go along with them in the cause of ultimate peace. We must try to more fully understand the special problems of the poorer nations and recognize their attitudes toward them, which come as a result of their differing religious and cultural backgrounds; and we must go a little way in co-operating with them. To do this it would be necessary to publicize more fully the aims, objectives and methods of this loosely organized body which is UNESCO, and endeavour to have our people know more and understand more about it. It is therefore our duty to speak about it and support it on all occasions.
I do not know whether I should do this, but I am going to close on what might perhaps be considered an emotional note but one which I think is fundamental to our attitude in the continued and more enthusiastic support which we must give to UNESCO. It is to turn to that portion of the Bible where our Saviour summarizes the ten commandments into the well-known exhortation when he says.
Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.
This is the first and great commandment.
And the second is like unto it, thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
The Address-Mr. Bryce
And this is significant;
On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
There have been good men, the Christian missionaries, who have gone out from our western countries and done the best they could with the limited funds and materials at their disposal. Perhaps we as western nations, the have nations, might now consider ourselves lay missionaries and by our actions and our attitudes try to live up to the second portion of the exhortation, "Love thy neighbour as thyself".
Somewhere in the Bible, I think in Proverbs, there is a passage which goes something like this, "Wisdom is the principal thing, therefore get wisdom. But with all thy getting get understanding." And so we complete the circle. That is what UNESCO is, an organization for mutual understanding.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I would like to congratulate the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). I am sure the constituents who sent them here will be pleased to see that they were honoured in this way by the present government.
The speech from the throne this year does not offer very much to debate or to pass an opinion on which points to an early election. However, I would like to take this opportunity of bringing before the government certain things in the Selkirk constituency which could be corrected.
One great problem that farmers have today is that of getting sufficient cash with which to carry on. This situation has been made worse by the recent railway strike. Many farms still have grain lying out in the fields gradually deteriorating. I know of one farmer in my constituency who has oats lying in piles out in his fields. When he threshed and sold some of that grain it was graded 3CW; they were Rodney oats. They have been lying out in the fields since threshing time, and the only grade the crop could be given now would be No. 1 feed grain. The difference in price between the two grades I have mentioned is a matter of only a few cents per bushel, but this represents a great loss when you have a few thousand bushels to sell.
There are also certain points where the quota still is one bushel per acre. The farmers on whose behalf I am speaking are people who had no crop last year, or practically none. They are now facing a loss for a second year. At the beginning of the crop

The Address-Mr. Bryce year the constituency did not have the grades that were required. The Department of Trade and Commerce or the wheat board wanted No. 3 wheat or malting barley, and we had practically none of those grades in the constituency. Therefore I hope the minister will not forget the interlake country, as the people there did not sell any grain last year and they should have the opportunity now to unload some grain. They have lots of No. 5 wheat and coarse grains. I was assured by the minister the other day that with the settlement of the railway strike these grains would move steadily. We have both the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. running through the interlake country, and they should be able to help put some money in the pockets of these farmers.
In parts of the interlake country the farmers derive their living raising cattle, and they complain bitterly about the fluctuations that take place in cattle prices from time to time. There is no guarantee that the farmer is not going to take a loss on his cattle, and I think some system of guaranteed prices is therefore required.
The same can be said of hogs. For instance, in October, 1953, hogs on the Winnipeg market were $30.44, which was a pretty good price. In 1954 they were down to $20.81, a drop of $10 in about ten months. In 1955 they were about the same, $20.54; in fact in December of 1955 they dropped as low as $19.72. On today's market in Winnipeg they are up again to $29. These fluctuations in price are not good for the producer, the packer or the consumer, and if some arrangement could be made whereby the farmers, through a system of guaranteed prices, could be protected against loss I think we would have a far more regular supply of hogs and cattle coming on the market.
On different occasions when the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture have been considered I have talked about some form of marketing agency. When I came here in 1943 I talked about a livestock marketing board. Then I talked about a board of livestock commissioners. However, there always seemed to be some objection to that type of thing. Then there was the problem that such a plan would have to originate in the provinces. I think that is right; it has to start in the provinces. However, after raising cattle and a few hogs for 40 years in this country I am still convinced that we should have a livestock marketing organization, because it would have a steadying influence on the prices of livestock.
I admit that there are a lot of people against such a plan. However, I have turned the matter over in my mind, I have read

about it and made inquiries about it, and I still think something has to be done to stabilize the livestock industry. Auction sales have been tried in different parts of the west but they do not appear to be too successful, and the results have not been what the farmers were trying to achieve.
I was a member of a committee in Manitoba that gave considerable study to the livestock marketing situation. The Manitoba livestock committee, under the chairmanship of the late Gordon Allison, put the reasons for a livestock marketing policy before the Manitoba farmers but, as I have already said, to be successful it would have to take in a very large territory. One province alone would not make it a success. At the very least you would have to have the three prairie provinces.
I would put forward these reasons in support of a livestock marketing policy. There should be such a policy in order to get more security and stability in the marketing of livestock. With a more stable livestock policy more people would raise livestock on the farms; hence there would be more consumption of grasses and legumes, which in turn would tie in with the conservation program in order that our soil might be built up with humus and organic matter. Erosion would also be checked. In this way we would keep the soil on our farms at home and not have it blow away.
Such a policy would in time build up our soil and enrich the country so we could turn it over to our heirs or those who follow us in as good or better shape than when we took over its care. This soil is a sacred trust. It is also our livelihood. If properly instituted, a sound livestock policy would better the position of the producer, the consumer and the packer; in fact it would increase the amount of livestock that would be processed. Breeders would stand to gain too, as they would have an expanded market for their livestock right at home. In fact we would have everything to gain and nothing to loose. Forty years' experience in the purebred livestock game has taught some of us that when commercial prices drop purebred prices drop accordingly, so if we can through a little effort get a more stable policy we will gain by what we have to sell commercially.
We are tied to a different economy today than in the horse and buggy days. We depend on tractors and power machinery to do the job, and the gas bills have to be met. It is a different story from when you could bring in your power in the form of horseflesh from the straw stack a week or two before seeding, when you had your power right there.

Such a policy would also expand our farming operations so we could use our young people on the farms, instead of forcing them to go to the cities to find work for the entire year.
When the St. Lawrence seaway is completed we will have refrigeration right on our doorstep at the head of the lakes, where ocean-going liners can pick up these products and distribute them anywhere in the world, for it is much cheaper to ship by water than by rail. We have airplanes now that can deliver goods in 24 hours anywhere in the world. We would be able to distribute these products more rapidly wherever people wanted them. Remember, two-thirds of the people in the world never go to bed at night feeling that they have had enough to eat, and in some countries there are always people who are starving for food.
I appeal to the minister again to give this matter further consideration; to see if it would not be possible to set up a small commission to look into it and decide whether it is possible to institute a livestock marketing system so that prices will be maintained and we will not have these fluctuations that sometimes take place from day to day. You may have a snowstorm on Monday and the price will go up, and then on Wednesday the price is away down. Fluctuations like that should not take place.
I wonder whether the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who was here a minute ago, has any information to give the house regarding the Disabled Persons Act. I have spoken to the minister at different times and asked him if he was sure that every province was administering the act in the same way. I said that some provinces were very strict in their administration of the act while others seemed more human, although the minister had previously explained that the regulations were drawn up in co-operation with the provinces.
He also stated that a conference was to be held last October. I am wondering if that conference took place, and if he could tell us anything about the discussion; whether any new amendments have been proposed or arrangements made to improve the act. As it is today a man or woman has to be confined to bed or unable to put on their own clothes before deriving benefit under this act. I wish the minister would give more consideration to this problem, as there are many disabled people who cannot earn their bread and butter and who are unable to receive any benefit from the act. I voted for the act when it was brought in; I thought then we were getting an act which was going to help take care of people who could not earn their own living.
The Address-Mr. Bryce
I do not wish to take the time of the house by dwelling further on the subject of old age pensions as most hon. members have already drawn the attention of the government to the need for an increase in the pension rate. I think that feeling is widespread in this house; people everywhere have been getting up and asking for increased old age pensions. When everybody is agreed, and the attention of the government has been drawn to this matter, then I think a reform is long overdue. The $40 which an aged citizen gets today has the value of only $20 compared with purchasing power in the past, and in the light of the continual rise in the cost of living which is taking place it is essential that the government should give immediate consideration to providing a decent living for those people who have helped to build the Canada that we inherit today.
Equally important is the subject of blind persons' pensions. A single blind person receives a pension of only $40 a month and, moreover, he is allowed to earn only another $40 before having the extra money deducted from his pension. These blind people are subject to the high cost of present day living in the same manner as those of us who are fortunate enough to have full sight, yet they do not receive any extra allowance for the extra cost that blindness imposes. Once again I appeal to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to give serious consideration to the plight of the disabled person, the blind person and the old age pensioner. It appears that in our efforts to build a better Canada we are inclined to forget the people who need help most.
I would like also to take the opportunity at this time to draw the attention of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to the problem of Indians leaving the reserves and finding work around the towns. This is a development which I am sure everyone is delighted to see, but it does present problems which I think the minister should straighten out before they develop into a major difficulty. I know the minister is aware of the situation because I have talked to him about it, with particular regard to its effect upon the town of Selkirk.
This is what happens. The Indian comes to town and finds work. Naturally, he gets along all right while work is plentiful. However, there comes a time when work is scarce and he cannot find funds on which to keep going. Usually he applies to the Indian agent and gets rations with which to carry on until he finds another job. This job may last a month or six weeks, after which he draws rations again. The process can carry on for one year, at the end of which time he is directed to


The Address-Mr. Bryce the town lor relief because he has been in residence in the town-Selkirk, for example -for one year.
This is where the main problem arises. Does he cease to be the responsibility of the Indian affairs branch at this stage? Remember, he is still a treaty Indian. Will the Indian affairs branch reimburse the town for the rations they supply to the Indian while he is a resident, say, of Selkirk? The same problem arises in other directions, and I am still talking about the treaty Indian. Should he fall sick after his 12 months' residence in town, will the Indian affairs branch pay any hospital or doctors' bills incurred by him during his sickness, or is the town expected to assume this responsibility? There is also the problem presented when an Indian falls sick while he is away from the reserve or when he is working away from home. Only recently we had some discussion as to who was responsible for hospital bills incurred by Indians in the Selkirk constituency. In my way of reading the Indian Act the treaty Indian is a ward of the Canadian government and is the responsibility of the government.
I would think that an Indian who belongs to a band and who has a band number would be a treaty Indian and, as such, would be the responsibility of the Indian affairs branch. In the recommendations made to the house by the Indian committee of both houses, which sat for three years, it was suggested that all phases of the Indian affairs branch should fall under one head and not be divided up as at the present time. The recommendation reads as follows:
. . . administrative improvements which could be effected without the revision of existing legislation and which, when put into effect, would remove some of the causes out of which arise grievances and complaints of many Indians. There are still some "administrative improvements" which your committee deems advisable. Your committee, therefore, again recommends that the administration of all aspects of Indian affairs be placed under one ministerial head.
I do not think that recommendation has ever been given any consideration. The minister, when he speaks on his estimates, will I am sure be able to answer these questions. The committee went even further and suggested that the director of the Indian affairs branch should be named a commissioner who should have the rank of deputy minister, and should have at least two assistant commissioners of whom one should be a Canadian of Indian descent. Perhaps in the near future the minister will have an opportunity of telling the house just how many of these recommendations have been acted upon, and what progress is being made to incorporate them into the Indian Act.

There is another question which presents considerable worry to the Indians, and that is the question of treaty rights and obligations. I talked about this on a previous occasion, because I think it is something that should be settled once and for all. This is something which was recommended by the Indian committee, and I quote the recommendation they made:
That a commission in the nature of a claims commission be set up with the least possible delay, to inquire into the terms of all Indian treaties in order to discover and determine, definitely and finally, such rights and obligations as are therein involved and, further, to assess and settle finally and in a just and equitable manner all claims or grievances which have arisen thereunder.
I hope the minister will be able to do something about these various problems to which I have drawn his attention. At the time of my first trip to the north country in 1943, that is up to Norway House, the conditions of the Indians were in a deplorable state, but there has since then been remarkable improvement in many ways. The new hospital is a wonderful achievement, and I hope the improvement will continue.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that one of the major domestic problems facing parliament this session is inflation. I also think some method must be found of bringing it under control. I look forward to hearing the statement which the Minister of Finance today promised to make on the subject at a later date.
There are many Canadians who are not particularly concerned about inflation, possibly because they do not realize the dangers inherent in the present situation, and also, probably, because the kind of inflation we have in Canada today is not of the extreme variety such as that which Germany experienced after world war I. Rather what we have in this country today is a sort of creeping inflation. But even though it is combined with rising standards of living and with widening opportunities in some cases, it is month by month gradually and insidiously eroding the value of our Canadian dollar.
Every hon. member realizes, I know, that in the past year Canada experienced one of her best years economically. When the final figures of production, consumption and prosperity are compiled I suppose they will show that, materially, Canada did better than any other nation in the world. Employment reached new levels in 1956. Our gross national product went up by leaps and bounds. Trade improved, wages increased and so on. In short, Canada has been literally bursting at the seams economically. Yet authorities who

should know tell us that the very vigour of the economic boom has given rise to factors which, if not controlled, could wipe out many of the economic gains which we have experienced since the end of the war.
With such prosperity prevalent throughout the country, I suppose it is natural that the average man in the street does not worry too much about inflation. As a matter of fact, in the early years of an inflationary spiral most people rather like it. It offers jobs for everyone at steadily increasing wages. It offers increasing dollar values for property. It offers opportunities to make easy money by speculating in things of real value. Yet, Mr. Speaker, inflation is like a thief in the night. It hurts most those who can least afford to be hurt. It takes a substantial bite today out of the wages of every workingman in this country. It works great hardship on those who are trying to live on fixed incomes, because the value of their savings is gradually decreasing.
In the past 50 years many nations have travelled the road to inflation, and most of them have travelled it to disaster. It seems to me that this parliament should take every possible action at this session to make sure that Canada does not travel the same road to recession or to depression.
One of the most obvious danger signals is our cost of living index increase. The last figure I saw was for October, when the cost of living index was 120.3 as compared with 100 in 1949. It showed an increase of 3.4 points in the eleven months preceding October.
What is even more alarming, I think, is the prospect for the next six months. There are some who hope that the inflationary fires will burn out before any additional government action is necessary. Personally I think that hope is wishful thinking. Last year our investment program was roughly $8 billion. If I understand the situation correctly, the figure will be substantially higher during the current year. I think that fact will inevitably increase the demand for labour and materials, and will bring additional pressure on our general price levels.
I know that for many months, Mr. Speaker, our government has recognized the dangers, and that it has taken some action. In cooperation with the Bank of Canada it has adopted what is known or has come to be known as a tight money policy. I certainly do not set myself up as an economist but, as I understand it, the present tight money policy does not arise from a contraction of money or of bank credit. The supply of money is about the same as it was about a year ago. Central bank policy, in co-operation
The Address-Mr. Thatcher with our banks, has been directed toward maintaining the volume of money at the same level as that of a year ago, and restraining any further expansion of credit. With the supply of money limited and with the demand for it practically insatiable, naturally the law of supply and demand has come into effect and interest rates have gone up. I think hon. members on all sides of the house would agree that the higher interest rates have been at least partially effective in discouraging additional business expansion financed by bank credit.
Personally I support wholeheartedly the steps which have been taken so far by the government to deal with these inflationary tendencies. Every country in the western world, I think, has taken similar steps. I am quite sure that if my hon. friends in' the Conservative party were sitting on the government side, they would take the same kind of action.
The primary purpose of the monetary measures taken by the Bank of Canada has been to extend the period of our boom and to protect the Canadian people against any economic bust. The rapidly rising interest rates, of course, have hurt in some quarters, but the hardships which they have inflicted are as nothing compared to what the hardships would be if this government adopted an easy money policy.
There are some fields which have been adversely affected. Housing and municipal finance have been mentioned. Perhaps there will have to be some adjustments in these fields. Naturally there have been complaints about this tight money policy from companies whose plans for expansion are hampered, but I think the government has put the over-all welfare of the nation ahead of political expediency in this particular instance. As a matter of fact it seems to me that there are indications today, and a good many of them, that the tight money policy of this government may have to be extended.
When the original Bank of Canada Act was formulated and designed, commercial banks extended most commercial credit. Today that is no longer the case in many instances. There are many other companies today which extend credit in large volume. I refer to finance companies, small loan companies, insurance companies, mortgage companies, credit unions and even government agencies.
It is quite true that an appeal has been made to these various organizations to restrict credit voluntarily, but I do not think such an appeal is adequate. Today there are many companies of the nature I have described which are still extending credit almost without limit. If inflation in Canada is

The Address-Mr. Thatcher to be controlled, I believe the government should set up a co-ordinated set of policies, principles and regulations which would govern all the various components of our financial system, and not the banks alone. Such a policy should be aimed at making our entire financial situation responsive to the actions of the Bank of Canada.
Perhaps I am wrong, Mr. Speaker, but it seems to me that there is another step which should be taken at the present time. Unless retail prices show some indication of stopping their upward spiral I believe the government must consider taking steps to curb credit at the retail level. A requirement of 25 per cent or 33J per cent down on all credit sales would not be popular, but I think it would be effective in temporarily postponing the demand for automobiles, appliances, furniture and the like. It could help to curb consumer demand with a minimum of hardship to anyone.
There is yet another step I should like to see the government take. I cannot help feeling today, as I have felt for 10 years, that parliament is sometimes prone to spend money too easily. How can we expect Canadian businessmen and Canadian industry in this period of emergency to use restraint in spending if we in this parliament, on all sides, allow the expenses which we should control to increase by several hundreds of millions of dollars each year? I think it is obvious, that government demands for manpower, government demands for materials, are just as responsible for pushing up prices as are the demands of industry. It seems to me, therefore, that governments at all three levels, federal, provincial and municipal, during the next few months should set an example to industry and private citizens by keeping their spending at a practical minimum.
What about family allowances? What should we do about them?
I am always amazed at the ability of socialist theorists to offer destructive criticism.
Should we cut down family allowances?

Most economists, I think, would agree that one of the major contributing factors to inflation today is a shortage of manpower. Parliament would be accentuating that shortage of manpower if it adds to the number of civil servants unnecessarily. Perhaps no one in the house will agree with me, but I think during the present emergency the Minister of Finance might be wise to freeze the number of civil servants at its present level.

What about tax policy? For many years in this house, as hon. members know, I have urged the Minister of Finance to bring about tax reductions, and I continue to believe that such a policy is desirable and urgent. I would be the first to admit that in this inflationary period perhaps this shortterm picture has altered. Last March the minister budgeted, I think, for a surplus of $113 million. It seems now that the surplus will reach $300 million. Surely a large and substantial part of that surplus should be used for debt reduction, and I commend such a policy to the minister as being anti-inflationary.
What of the remainder of the surplus? Personally I say this with respect, I would rather the minister did not leave the balance of this surplus lying around because there are too many hon. members who can find ways of spending it. I should like to see, as I say-
Too many old age pensioners now?
I shall tell my hon. friend that so far as the old age pensioners are concerned, they may be taken care of sooner than my hon. friend wishes.
What about the means test for old age pensions?

I am glad to talk about the means test. For 10 years now I have listened to C.C.F. members advocate the removal of the means test down here in Ottawa, yet out in Saskatchewan they have the most rigid means test in the whole world, on their supplementary allowance to pensioners.
Do you favour abolishing the means test?

Mr. Speaker, I said that I favoured tax reduction if it is feasible at the moment. If economists tell us it is too dangerous to put this extra purchasing power into the hands of consumers at the present time, then I believe some method should be found to give the public the benefit of tax reduction on a postponed basis. Perhaps some kind of deferred savings certificate could be issued by the government which would not be redeemable for three years or five years.
I say that inflationary tendencies are not out of control in this country, but there are danger signals on the horizon. The Minister of Finance knows better than anyone that combating inflation is neither an easy task nor a popular one, but every Canadian will be adversely affected if parliament ignores the problem. In the period ahead we must

look to the Minister of Finance for leadership, yet others must also accept their responsibilities. Industrialists and merchants must be moderate in their pricing policies; labour must be moderate in its demands for wage increases, and members of parliament must be moderate in the demands they make on the Minister of Finance for increased expenditures. If we give the minister that kind of co-operation I think we can hold inflation within bounds, reasonable bounds, during 1957. I hope the minister will consider the suggestions I have made, and I hope he may find some of them feasible.

I listened with great interest, Mr. Speaker, to the excellent speech we have just heard. I wonder if the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and who appears to identify the government of Canada with the Bank of Canada, could point out any action which the government of Canada, as distinguished from the Bank of Canada, has taken to deal with any inflationary trend about which he has talked?
I am a backbench member, and I would not suggest policy.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Hanna) and seconder (Mr. Robi-chaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. This year the speech from the throne dealt mainly with foreign affairs, and the two speeches made in this house on Monday last by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Health and Welfare emphasized the importance of this subject.
There has been so much said during the emergency session and this session about the United Nations police force in Egypt that one wonders what magic wand the United Nations is going to use now to accomplish in the Middle East what the United Nations has dismally failed to accomplish in the past 10 years of its existence. If one is brutally frank he is forced to admit that the United Nations has been a dismal failure to date. It has not had any effective policy for dealing with the various problems that have affected the Middle East for many years. The problems of the Middle East are not new and they are not going to be solved overnight. This powder keg has been in existence for years. Various matters affecting the Middle East have been before the United Nations for years. The score to date is just nil.
I shall cite one instance, and that is the plight of the hundreds of thousands of Arab refugees. These people became refugees on the day the state of Israel came into being.
The Address-Mr. G. S. White Years after this event took place we still find hundreds of thousands of these unfortunate people who are not re-established or resettled. You will find them in the Arab states of Lebanon, Syria and Jordan. These refugees, with their families, are living under the most deplorable conditions of utter poverty. From time to time every member in this house has received pamphlets and literature outlining the plight of these unfortunate people. This matter has been before the United Nations time and time again, and nothing has been done.
In the three Arab countries you will find large settlements of these refugees living in the most squalid conditions in large camps along the road between Baalbeck and Damascus; you will find them scattered along the highway from Damascus to Amman and in the vicinity of Jericho, Jerusalem, and in other parts of the Arab states. This one problem has been a festering sore for years, well known to all members of the United Nations, yet no action has been taken.
There have also been the old questions of the Gaza strip, the boundary line, the right of Egypt to block and to prevent Israeli ships going through the canal. As I said, these problems affecting this part of the world have been before the United Nations for years and little if anything has been done. It seems to me that the United Nations has proved itself utterly incapable of dealing with these problems which have simply screamed to be settled; and today, after years of senseless and useless debate and passing resolutions that would stretch around the world, but taking no action, we are asked to base the hope for peace in the world on the action of the United Nations in sending a small police force to the Middle East.
The present force, we are told, is composed of about 5,500 men, of whom only some 1,100 are Canadians. To me, 20 per cent of the entire force seems rather a large percentage for Canada. If you take from these 5,500 men the administrative staff, the medical, the army service corps, the signallers, the engineers and all the other services that go to make up a modern army brigade today, you will have very few men left to carry out the so-called police duties.
At page 174 of Hansard the Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
This has led to a demand in some quarters that somehow or other United Nations assembly should take action to enforce effectively its own recommendations. This of course ignores the fact that such compulsory enforcement procedure through the assembly is not in accordance with the terms of the charter as drafted.
That very clearly indicates that this small police force in Egypt has no authority to
318	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. G. S. White enforce anything. I would have liked very much if the Secretary of State for External Affairs had explained to the house in detail just what are the duties of this police force and what it has accomplished to date, if anything; and what military equipment this force has. I take it, if it is a police force, it is not to fight. What is it to do if it is attacked? What is it to do if fighting breaks out again between Israel and Egypt, or one of the other Arab states? How long is the force to remain there? I think the hon. member for Oxford clearly showed today that it is going to stay there just as long as Colonel Nasser will permit it to stay there.
What are the duties of this force as far as the canal is concerned? Can it be ordered out of Egypt at any time? And, of some importance to the Canadian taxpayers, what proportion of the entire cost of the more than 1,100 Canadian troops in Egypt is to be paid by Canada? The Secretary of State for External Affairs made very clear during the emergency session, and in his speech on Monday, that the police force is very restricted in its actions. He spoke on Monday. At page 175 of Hansard he tried to give the impression that the force had accomplished a great deal, and at page 176 he made this very significant statement:
But even within these limitations the United Nations force can, I think, play an important part in bringing about an honourable and enduring political settlement in the Palestine and Suez area.
Well, it would have been more interesting if the minister had only enlarged upon that and shown how this police force, with its limited powers, is able to bring about a settlement of any kind.
There are many people in Canada who believe that if Britain and France had not acted in the Suez, Russia would have moved in and today Russia would have been in complete control of the canal and the Middle East. Many people feel that the action of France and Britain was necessary to preserve their very existence, an action necessary in view of the previous feeble actions of the United Nations and the United States.
What happened? The Canadian government turned its back on France and Britain, and was described by some as being very bitter and severe. The true feeling of the Canadian government was well expressed by the Prime Minister on page 20 of Hansard of the emergency session, when he made that statement and by the manner in which he made it. The statement is as follows:
The era when the supermen of Europe could govern the whole world has and is coming pretty close to an end.
Well, I would like to tell the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External


Affairs that in the part of eastern Ontario where I reside the vast majority of Canadian people do not agree with or approve of the sentiment expressed in the words uttered by the Prime Minister; nor do they agree with the action of the Canadian government in not supporting France and Britain. I had hoped that at some time either the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs would tell the house and the country what, in their opinion, would have happened to the Suez canal and the Middle East if France and Britain had not acted. If the policy that the President of the United States recently submitted to congress had been declared earlier there would not, in my opinion, have been any crisis in the Middle East. Press despatches of today report the appearance of Secretary of State Dulles before a Senate committee, in which he said: State Secretary Dulles said today there would be "a very great likelihood" of United States troops fighting in the Middle East if congress rejects President Eisenhower's Middle East manifesto.
What they are pressing for is exactly the same action that France and Britain took. From the two speeches made on Monday by the two ministers one can judge that they have apparently seen the commonwealth in a new light, because it has been a long time, prior to Monday last, since anyone in this house has heard any minister of the crown make any complimentary remarks about the commonwealth. In fact it has been the usual practice of ministers to avoid any reference of any kind to the commonwealth, or to mention any of the benefits of the commonwealth to the entire world.
The speeches of the two ministers were remarkable in that they made some attempt to repair the damage done by the remarks of the Prime Minister in the emergency session. I do not think anybody is going to disagree with the remarks made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He spoke in most glowing terms about the commonwealth, what Britain had done in granting independence and self-government to former colonies. He mentioned the names of certain nations which will soon be members of the commonwealth. In my opinion these remarks were a well-deserved tribute to the statesmen of the United Kingdom, who only such a short time ago were described and classified by the Prime Minister as aggressors and the supermen of Europe.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, not to be outdone by his colleague, also praised the commonwealth and several times during his speech lauded the work of the commonwealth in every way. I should like to read two passages from his speech, at page

186 of Hansard. In referring to various countries in Asia the minister said:
I also told them that, as a member of the commonwealth, Canada felt that that instrument had in its very concept the opportunity of providing not only for the good of its constituents but for the welfare of all nations in the world, in Asia as well as elsewhere, who are prepared to understand its good intentions and purposes.
I congratulate the minister on having a view of that kind. He went on to say:
But my judgment would be that, for the most part, those who at the present time have to do with the conduct of government in those great countries recognized that in the consultations of prime ministers, in the consultations of commonwealth foreign ministers and in the collaboration that takes place in the United Nations, the commonwealth serves as a valuable instrument in a world that needs to move closer and closer together rather than diverge on an increasing scale.
I also congratulate the minister on those sentiments; but both ministers in their glowing words about the commonwealth overlooked one certain factor that was aptly pointed out yesterday by the hon. member for Kamloops, who indicated that not once in all the glowing references they made to the commonwealth did they mention the vital factor of the centre of commonwealth unity, loyalty to the crown.
In the speech from the throne there was no reference to any amendment to the Succession Duty Act, unless that reference was contained in the last few words where it mentioned that amendments to certain other acts would be submitted. I sincerely hope this act will be amended. It was mentioned last year in the speech from the throne, but no amendments were brought forward. In my opinion the present act should be revised in the light of changing economic conditions.
Conditions have changed considerably since the act was first introduced a long time ago. At the present time an estate of up to $50,000 is exempt from tax, but if the estate exceeds $50,000 it is taxable in its entirety. That appears most unfair to me, and I feel the exemption should be raised to at least $75,000 and this amount should be exempt from duty in any event. Every hon. member of this house who is a member of the legal profession knows from his own knowledge and has seen from his personal experience many instances of the effect of income tax and succession duties on income under wills or trusts, pensions, lump sum payments and other similar payments received by a surviving dependent, and are well aware of the hardship created.
One other matter in connection with succession duties is that of charitable bequests and charitable donations made within three years of the date of death, as well as unpaid
The Address-Mr. G. S. White subscriptions to charitable organizations. Many people feel that these should not be included in arriving at the value of an estate for the purpose of determining the initial rate of duty.
In regard to income tax, despite what has been said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I for one hope the Minister of Finance is going to raise the exemption of a married man to at least $3,000 and the exemption of a single person to at least $1,500, and consider a reasonable increase in exemptions for children. Everyone knows that inflation has greatly raised the cost of living, that municipal taxes have increased and that the price of everything the taxpayer has to buy is following an upward trend. The taxpayer is subject to many taxes which are hidden in the sale price tag.
The present exemption for children is only $150 in the case of a child in receipt of family allowance and $400 in the case of a child not receiving family allowance. How far will $400 a year go toward the support of a child over 16 years of age who is attending school or college? Even a casual examination of the prices of goods advertised in the newspapers today, including the prices of clothing, footwear and the other necessities of life, will indicate that an exemption of $400 is a small exemption indeed.
There is also the situation of many taxpayers who are living on fixed incomes. In many cases the income was fixed years ago when the dollar was worth a great deal more than it is worth today. The present rate of taxation and scale of exemption works a hardship on this type of taxpayer, and I suggest to the minister that he might well consider allowing an exemption of more than $500 to all taxpayers over the age of 65 years.
There was a short reference to agriculture in the speech from the throne which will not greatly encourage the Canadian farmer. The hon. member for Middlesex East very well placed the position of the farmer before the house in his remarks as recorded at page 85 of Hansard, when he showed that the Canadian farm economy is being exploited to provide markets for manufactured goods. Although Canada is a great producing nation many of our agricultural products are imported from abroad. Each year several million pounds of cheese are imported into Canada, fruit and vegetables are imported from the United States, tomatoes and tomato pulp are hauled across the ocean from Europe and then go by rail to marketing points where they compete with local products, although it is true we have certain tariffs that operate only on a seasonal basis.

The Address-Mr. G. S. White For instance, last year many hon. members received representations from turkey producers concerning the importation of turkeys from the United States which undersell the local market. I have a large number of turkey producers in my district, and I have received letters concerning this situation. Representations were made to the Minister of Agriculture last year by turkey producers.
Ask any farmer in Ontario today who is engaged in mixed farming concerning the great increase in the cost of every article he must purchase for the operation of his farm, including the increases in labour costs and municipal taxes, and compare these increases with the prices of the products he has for sale. Every rural newspaper carries notices and reports of meetings of the fast-growing farmers' union held in every county throughout Ontario. No doubt many hon. members have attended these meetings and discovered that in many cases they could not find much fault with the arguments put forth by the farmers. The farmers want only their fair share of the income of the nation. As many hon. members have already observed, because this is an election year something may be done for Canadian farmers.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word or two in support of those hon. members who have spoken on behalf of the Canadian veteran. I have in my hand the brief presented to the government by the Legion, and there are one or two matters I would like to mention. The Legion has made extremely reasonable requests the granting of which in many cases would not increase government expenditure in any way. For instance, they ask for an increase in the permissible ceiling, which is not going to cost the federal treasury one cent. They simply ask that the ceilings on total permissible incomes under the War Veterans' Allowance Act be increased to $1,200 per year for the single recipient and $2,000 per year for the married recipient. They further ask that the married rate of the war veterans' allowance be increased from $108 per month to $120 per month. They also ask that Canadian veterans of world war I whose overseas service was restricted to the United Kingdom be eligible for war veterans' allowance. This request is also most reasonable and one that has been submitted to the minister on many occasions.
The only other request I wish to mention is that respecting the present equity value of the home in which a war veterans allowance recipient resides. Such a veteran is now permitted to have an equity of up to $6,000. Every hon. member knows, from his knowledge of the value of property in his own


community, that $6,000 is a very low figure. The Legion asks that the figure be increased to $9,000. This again will not entail the outlay of one cent of public funds.
I realize that these requests have been made repeatedly to the minister, but I would point out to him that the present very cold spell means for many pensioners and veterans in receipt of war veterans allowance extra fuel, food and clothing which in many cases they can ill afford. The number of veterans who will receive a pension, if the pension is granted to veterans of world war I who served in England, is very small, and the amount of extra funds from the public treasury will not be very great. I sincerely hope that the Minister of Veterans Affairs and his parliamentary assistant will take some action at this session of parliament to implement the very fair and reasonable recommendations contained in the brief presented to the government by the Legion last fall.

Mr. Speaker, with your permission I should like to move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Shaw the debate was adjourned.
